front: Which regulations control most US commercial and dual-use exports, and which agency administers them?
back: The **Export Administration Regulations (EAR)**, 15 CFR Parts 730–774, administered by the Commerce Department's **Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS)**.
extra: Defense articles fall under the ITAR (State Department) instead. That is unlikely for a distributor, but it must be ruled out, not assumed.

front: In ECCN 3A001, what do the last three digits, 001, signal?
back: The **reason for control**. 001 is in the **0xx series: national security**. The 1xx series is missile technology and 2xx nuclear nonproliferation.
extra: Also 3xx chemical and biological weapons, 9xx anti-terrorism and other controls. Reasons can overlap: the first digit shows the one that takes precedence (0 for an item controlled for both national security and missile technology), and the entry lists every reason to check against the Country Chart.
reuses: US export: in an ECCN, what do the last-three-digit series 0xx, 1xx and 2xx signal?

front: What designation does an item get when it is subject to the EAR but matches no entry on the Commerce Control List?
back: **EAR99**. Most everyday commercial goods are EAR99 and usually need no export license.
extra: Common mistake: 'EAR99 means no license, ever'. An EAR99 item can still need a license for an embargoed destination, a prohibited end use or a restricted party.

front: Besides the item's ECCN or EAR99 status, which three facts decide whether an export needs a license?
back: The **destination** (Commerce Country Chart and embargoes), the **end user** (restricted-party lists) and the **end use** (prohibited uses). 15 CFR Part 732 sets out the steps.
extra: License determinations stay with the Senior. Your exports work is the data behind them: a wrong ECCN, destination or party record produces a wrong answer.
reuses: US export: which four facts drive an EAR license determination?

front: What is Electronic Export Information (EEI), and what proves that it was filed?
back: Export data filed in the **Automated Export System (AES)** under the Foreign Trade Regulations (15 CFR Part 30). AES returns an **Internal Transaction Number (ITN)** as proof of filing.
extra: The USPPI, usually the US seller, is responsible for accurate EEI data; records are kept 5 years (15 CFR 30.10). An exempt shipment carries an exemption legend instead of an ITN, such as 'NOEEI 30.37(a)'.

front: What is a Schedule B number, and what may an EEI filing report instead for most goods?
back: The Census Bureau's **10-digit export classification**, based on the HS. For most goods the EEI may report the **10-digit HTSUS import number** instead, unless that number is flagged invalid for export.
extra: The first 6 digits are the HS subheading, as in the HTSUS. Schedule B or ECCN data gaps in item master data are typical exports backlog items for you.
reuses: US export: what is a Schedule B number?

front: Export to Country X, no license: PART-A $1,600 + PART-B $1,200 (same Schedule B number), KIT-100 $2,000 (another). What needs EEI, if anything?
back: **EEI is required**, but it reports only the Schedule B number of PART-A and PART-B: $1,600 + $1,200 = $2,800, over US$2,500. KIT-100's number totals $2,000, so it is exempt and left off.
extra: The test is per Schedule B number within one shipment (one USPPI, consignee and conveyance), not per line or on the shipment total: add the lines that share a number. Domestic and foreign-origin goods are tested separately. Licensed items and other mandatory cases need EEI at any value.
reuses: US export: how is the US$2,500 EEI exemption tested?

front: Most US exports to Canada need no EEI, even above US$2,500. Which exports to Canada still need it?
back: Goods that need a **license** (and other mandatory filing cases), goods **stored in Canada** for later export elsewhere, and goods **moving through Canada** to a third country (15 CFR 30.36).
extra: Destination matters as much as value: a shipment that needs EEI to Country X is generally exempt when it goes to Canada.
reuses: US export: when does a shipment to Canada need EEI?

front: In your first 90 days as maker on exports backlog items, which three kinds of decision stay with the Senior?
back: **License determinations**, **restricted-party screening match decisions** and **voluntary disclosures**. The Senior is your checker and remains the owner of exports.
extra: A possible screening match is put on hold and escalated, never cleared by a hire. Filing decisions and anything with a regulatory deadline also stay with the Senior. Suitable items for you: data corrections, master-data fixes with review, report tweaks, documentation and reconciliations.

front: What is a standard cost, and what is it compared with?
back: A **predetermined cost per item** (material, freight, duty, overhead) that values inventory and cost of goods sold until the next cost update. **Actual costs** are compared with it; the differences are variances such as PPV.
extra: Why a stale standard matters: when duty or freight changes and the standard does not, the difference lands in variance accounts instead of in item cost, and reported margins absorb it.
reuses: Standard cost: what is a standard cost?

front: What does landed cost add on top of the supplier's price?
back: Everything it takes to get the item into our warehouse: **international freight and insurance**, **duties and customs fees**, and **brokerage and inland freight**.
extra: Recoverable import taxes (Canada GST, Mexico IVA) are normally not a cost: confirm with Finance and never add them by default. Freight is allocated by a documented driver, such as weight, kept the same between cycles unless Finance agrees a change.
reuses: Landed cost: what is landed cost?

front: KIT-100 (US import): FOB $40.00, ocean freight $3.00, insurance $0.20 per unit; hypothetical duty 5% ad valorem. What is the duty per unit?
back: **$2.00** = 5% × $40.00. US customs value excludes international freight and insurance identified separately, so the duty base is $40.00, not $43.20 or the $46.50 landed cost.
extra: Common mistake: rate × landed cost (5% × $46.50 = $2.325, about $2.33) overstates duty on every item from that lane. The cost cycle catches it with a hand check of items per import country against the duty base rules.
reuses: Landed cost (US): why is an ad valorem duty not calculated on landed cost?

front: PART-A sells for $20.00 with a $14.00 landed standard. A new hypothetical 10% duty applies to its $10.00 customs value. What happens to its margin?
back: Duty adds **$1.00** (10% × $10.00), so landed cost becomes $15.00. Gross margin falls from $6.00 (**30%**) to $5.00 (**25%**) unless the price changes.
extra: This is the Tariff-Impact Model's logic: only the duty changes, with freight, fees and prices held constant. Its new standard is an estimate for decisions; the Oracle load still goes through the full standard cost cycle.
reuses: Landed cost: an item sells for $20.00 with a $14.00 landed standard. A new 10% duty applies on its $10.00 customs value. What happens to margin?

front: In a standard cost cycle, which two sign-offs must be in place before anything loads to Oracle?
back: The **checker's review** (the Manager; the Senior for duty-rate or classification questions) and **Finance's written approval** of the cost changes and the revaluation estimate. The maker never approves their own file.
extra: Why: a wrong standard instantly misstates inventory value and margins. The rule continues after day 90. The approved file is locked read-only; any later change is a new version with a new review and approval.
reuses: Standard cost: why does every cost update need maker-checker review?

front: In a standard cost cycle, what happens to the collected inputs at the end of Phase 2, before anything is calculated?
back: They are **frozen** (by default at T-15): the input pack is saved read-only with every extract's timestamp and linked on the Jira epic. Later changes wait for the next cycle unless Finance and the Manager approve.
extra: Why: the checker must review exactly what the cost file was built from. A change after the freeze breaks that link, and the loaded costs no longer match what was reviewed.
source: Standard cost update checklist, Phases 1 and 2

front: During the first 90 days, who posts the standard cost update to Oracle production?
back: **Whoever posts it today** keeps doing it. Hire B prepares and checks the cost inputs as maker; an Oracle cost update is not a tool a hire can own.
extra: Any exception needs written approval from the Manager, the Finance controller and ERP security, covers only the cost-update function, and must pass the segregation-of-duties check. Maker-checker applies either way.

front: What must you show at the day-60 review for the Manager to grant production change rights for your owned tool?
back: All six **'owns one tool'** points on the diagram, including **one end-to-end run**, a **tool doc** the Manager could follow alone, and **one change tested** in the test copy through a change request.
extra: Point 2 also means you can name the tool's known failure modes and how to recover from each. The rights then cover only that tool, and only through change control.

front: For the day-60 'owns one tool' criteria, which end-to-end run of the tool counts?
back: One run is enough, **either** supervised in production with the current knowledge holder, who executes every production write, **or** alone on a test copy.
extra: Write the tool doc's run steps while you do them, with screenshots. Mark any step you did not perform yourself 'not yet verified'.

front: For day 60 you propose an e2open disposition for your owned tool. Which options can it take?
back: **Replace, interface, retire or keep**, or **TBD** with the open question written down. The disposition is confirmed after the e2open kickoff.
extra: Business rules hidden in the tool's code must not be lost in the migration: list them in the tool doc so they reach the requirements.

front: Before day 60, you have changed and tested your owned tool in the test copy. Who puts the change into production?
back: **The Manager**, after the checker review and approval. Before the day-60 review you have no production write access, so you never deploy a change yourself.
extra: From the day-60 review, if the Manager grants change rights, you may implement changes to that one tool yourself, still only through a change request with a checker.

front: Which test must every tool change request include, whatever the change?
back: A **regression test**: run the old and new versions on the same input and confirm that the only differences are the ones you intended.
extra: Example: a fix to keep HTS numbers as 10-digit text changed exactly the 312 truncated rows, only in the HTS column, and nothing else. Attach the comparison to the Jira issue.

front: Who is the checker for changes to a tool you own, before and after day 60?
back: **The Manager**, always. Owning a tool never means approving your own change: the maker is never the checker.
extra: The checker reviews the code or configuration diff, the test evidence, the impact rows and the rollback plan, and records the decision on the Jira issue. No approval, no implementation.
source: Change request template (Who uses it; section 10)

front: A tool change's first production run goes wrong. Which part of the change request, written before implementing, says what to do?
back: The **rollback plan**: the result that triggers it, who decides, the steps and the time they take, and where the verified backup is.
extra: Confirm the backup exists before you implement. With a written plan you restore the previous version in minutes instead of improvising. Plan the clean-up of any outputs the faulty version already sent to a broker or Finance.
source: Change request template, step 7 and section 8

front: How is a tool change approved when the tool is sending wrong data to a broker right now?
back: As an **Emergency** change: the Manager's verbal go-ahead, a checker review the same day, and the change request template completed within 1 working day.
extra: Emergency is only for production producing wrong data now. If a workaround has already stopped the bad data, it is a Normal change: test fully first.
